metadata.note: Youngstown, OH was a five-railroad steel-town hub -- Erie, Pittsburgh & Lake Erie, Pennsylvania, Baltimore & Ohio, and New York Central all served it, with 16 daily passenger trains crossing at one of the busiest non-interlocked railroad crossings in the U.S. Three distinct historic corridors are covered here, though only two are distinct on the map (see correction below). (1) The Pittsburgh & Lake Erie Railroad, Pittsburgh-New Castle-Youngstown, opened Feb 10 1879 -- New York Central took a minority stake immediately and full control by 1889, making the P&LE a NYC property in all but name; this is very likely also the corridor NYC's own separately-branded Youngstown service and the Baltimore & Ohio's Youngstown trains used, since the B&O secured trackage rights over the P&LE between McKeesport and New Castle in 1934 rather than building its own parallel line -- those two railroads' Youngstown access is not separately traced here, as it physically rides this same right-of-way. (2) The Pennsylvania Railroad's Pittsburgh, Youngstown and Ashtabula (PY&A), tracing back to the 1853-chartered Ashtabula and New Lisbon Railroad, extended from Youngstown to Niles (continuing toward Ashtabula and a B&O connection at 'BOANNA' near Niles Junction); its named train, the Clevelander, ran until 1961, and the whole branch was abandoned in 1975 after the 1968 Penn Central merger made it redundant to NYC's superior line. (3) The Erie's Cleveland and Mahoning Valley Railroad, Cleveland-Warren-Youngstown, chartered 1848, completed 1857 -- opening the Mahoning Valley coal fields to Lake Erie ports -- and leased 1863 to the Atlantic & Great Western Railroad (see atlantic_great_western_jamestown.geojson, which covers that company's Salamanca-Dayton broad-gauge line and gained Cleveland access via this same C&MV lease). GEOMETRY METHODOLOGY / KNOWN LIMITATION (added 2026-08-23): all three were real-traced independently through OpenStreetMap active/abandoned-rail data (Overpass API, shortest-path graph search). For the Pittsburgh-Youngstown stretch, the P&LE and PY&A traces came back essentially identical (within meters of each other for the entire ~64 miles) -- NOT because the two railroads actually shared track (they were rival companies, NYC vs. PRR, and would not have), but because the real historic PY&A right-of-way was physically removed after its 1975 abandonment and no longer exists in any mappable form, even as disused track. Only one corridor survives today -- the P&LE's -- so both Overpass traces converged on it. The PY&A feature's Pittsburgh-Youngstown portion should therefore be read as an APPROXIMATION riding the P&LE's surviving alignment, not independent confirmation of the historic PY&A's own separate route; only its Youngstown-Niles extension (where the P&LE didn't go) is a genuinely distinct trace.

metadata.rule4_split_2026_08_24: Rule 4 ownership split, 2026-08-24. cmv-cleveland-youngstown was one feature in one colour spanning four owners; its Erie (1941-1960), Erie Lackawanna (1960-1976) and Conrail (1976-1977) years are now separate features sharing identical geometry, coloured for the operator that actually ran the trains. The Erie and the DL&W merged October 17 1960 to form the Erie Lackawanna -- neither became the other. The pre-1941 Cleveland & Mahoning / A&GW years are left as a single composite feature: the A&GW lease of 1863 is an ownership change that arguably deserves its own split too, but the A&GW has no canonical colour anywhere in data/ yet, so that one is left for a future pass.
not_yet_sourced: SOURCE CONFLICT -- last day of the Cleveland-Youngstown commuter train. Wikipedia's 'Cleveland commuter rail' gives January 14 1977 under Conrail; the Encyclopedia of Cleveland History says the service ended in 1976 when the State of Ohio and Conrail declined further subsidy. 1977 is drawn.

The previous end date of 1970 for this branch was explicitly flagged in its own note as approximated from the wider Erie system's discontinuance. It was wrong: the Cleveland-Youngstown commuter train outlived every other EL passenger train by seven years. Corrected 2026-08-24.
metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.
metadata.nyc_company_split: 2026-08-24: compound "predecessor / New York Central Railroad" company strings split per CLAUDE.md Rule 4. The legend groups on the exact company string (app.js railroadsInView), so a compound string drew as a separate railroad from the New York Central even for years the NYC itself ran the trains. Each feature is now split at the date its own segment note names the new operator, into features with identical geometry: the predecessor keeps its name and colour for the earlier years, and the NYC-operated years become "New York Central Railroad" at #5C677D. The Pittsburgh and Lake Erie and the Big Four were renamed but NOT split -- both were NYC-controlled yet stayed separately operated railroads under their own names, so they keep their own legend row.

segments.note: Traces back to the Ashtabula and New Lisbon Railroad, chartered 1853 (construction delayed by the Civil War and economic conditions); consolidated over subsequent decades into the Pittsburgh, Youngstown and Ashtabula (PY&A) under Pennsylvania Railroad ownership; frequency estimated, unsourced. segments.note: Absorbed into the Erie Railroad system by 1941. The Erie had moved its Cleveland passenger trains into the Terminal Tower (Cleveland Union Terminal) in 1949, renting tracks from the New York Central, and closed its old station in the flats. The Erie ceased to exist October 17 1960, merging with the DL&W to form the Erie Lackawanna. Frequency estimated, unsourced.

segments.note: Commuter-only from 1964: a single weekday round trip, 66.2 miles and thirteen stations between Cleveland Union Terminal and Youngstown via Solon, Aurora and Warren. When EL discontinued its last long-distance trains January 6 1970 this became the railroad's only remaining passenger service, and the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio refused permission to drop it. Erie Lackawanna went bankrupt in 1972 and passed to Conrail April 1 1976. Headway of one train each way per weekday is documented, not estimated.

segments.note: Conrail took over the Erie Lackawanna April 1 1976 and closed EL's Cleveland offices; ridership on the commuter train dropped sharply and the last run was January 14 1977 -- the final passenger train ever to use Cleveland Union Terminal. One source (Encyclopedia of Cleveland History) instead says the service ended in 1976 when Ohio and Conrail declined to subsidise it further; the January 14 1977 date is used here. Headway of one train each way per weekday is documented, not estimated.
